prompt: What does a case study's Constraints section add that a four-part README (Problem/Solution/Architecture/Demo) has no equivalent for?
choices: The exact commands needed to install and run the project
The real limits that shaped the build, such as time, team size, or data you didn't control
The exact file layout and data flow between modules
A terminal transcript or GIF proving the demo actually ran

prompt: A case study's main prose is written primarily for which reader?
choices: A fellow engineer who will audit your implementation details and jargon
A hiring manager or reviewer skimming for impact and judgment, not mechanism
An automated resume-parsing script
The open-source maintainer who reviewed your pull request

prompt: Which of these is an honest, falsifiable metric rather than a vague unquantified claim?
choices: "Blazing-fast, enterprise-grade routing engine"
"Cut /route's measured p95 latency from ~190ms to ~9ms on cache hits, measured with hey against the live Fly.io URL"
"Built a scalable and robust backend trusted by hikers everywhere"
"A powerful, production-ready API"

prompt: TrailLink's cache-invalidation bug (a stale adjacency list after POST /segments) has a natural home in which part of the case study, where the original four-part README had no equivalent section for it at all?
choices: Demo
Architecture
Decisions and Lessons Learned
License

prompt: Why does a case study typically skip reproducing the README's full file-by-file Architecture breakdown?
choices: Because the Architecture section is factually wrong
Because a hiring manager skimming for impact and judgment doesn't need implementation-level file layout; that detail still lives in the README the case study links to
Because case studies may not mention any code
Because Architecture sections cannot legally be reused

prompt: A solo capstone has no real production traffic to measure. What's the honest way to fill in its Metrics section?
choices: Invent a plausible-sounding number so the section isn't empty
Run your own measurable test (a load test, a coverage run, a timed before/after) and report that number scoped to exactly what you tested, or state plainly that no quantified number exists yet
Copy a benchmark figure from a well-known open-source project in the same space
Delete the Metrics section and hope a reviewer doesn't notice

prompt: The Black 'Preview flag' pull request, drawn from this track's Sustained Open-Source Contribution module, mainly demonstrates which point about open-source work as case-study material?
choices: Any merged PR, even a one-line doc fix, is automatically strong case-study material
Incorporating specific maintainer feedback into a concrete architectural decision is itself a case-study-worthy Decision, not just a resume line
Open-source contributions should never appear in a portfolio case study
The Preview flag system has no relevance to how the PR should be written up

prompt: What is the main structural difference between a portfolio card and a case study for the same project?
choices: The case study is shorter and uses no headings at all
The card is a roughly 30-second skim-level pitch; the case study is the deeper 2-3 minute read a hiring manager opens after the card earns the click
They are the same document, just published at two different URLs
The card quantifies impact with real numbers and the case study never does
